title: What is the difference between Kubernetes HPA (more/fewer replicas by load), VPA (adjust a pod's CPU/memory), and Cluster Autoscaler (add/remove nodes), can HPA and VPA be used together safely, and when do you reach for event-driven/queue-based scaling (KEDA — e.g. scale workers by queue depth rather than CPU)?
shortTitle: The difference between Kubernetes HPA, VPA, and Cluster Autoscaler, and when to use KEDA

s1_definition.profdef: These are three complementary Kubernetes autoscalers operating at different layers. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pod replicas based on observed load like CPU or custom metrics — scaling out and in. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts the CPU and memory requests of individual pods — scaling up and down the size of each pod. The Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes whole nodes from the cluster when pods cannot be scheduled or nodes sit idle. KEDA is an event-driven add-on that lets the HPA scale on external signals such as queue depth or Kafka lag rather than CPU, which fits bursty, queue-based workloads that CPU alone reacts to too slowly.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's processing floor. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is the policy of opening more identical counters when the queue grows and closing them when it shrinks. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler is the policy of giving each individual clerk a bigger desk and more drawers because the work each one does turned out to need more space than you first allotted. The Cluster Autoscaler is the facilities team that leases another floor of the building when there is no room left for new counters, and gives back a floor when it is empty to save rent. KEDA is the special rule for the back office: instead of watching how hard the clerks are sweating, it watches the physical height of the pile of pending forms and pulls in workers the instant the pile grows, even from zero, which is exactly right for batch paperwork that arrives in bursts.
s1_definition.oneliner: HPA adds more pods, VPA makes each pod bigger, Cluster Autoscaler adds more nodes, and KEDA scales on event signals like queue depth instead of CPU — different layers for different problems.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are three complementary Kubernetes autoscalers operating at different layers. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pod replicas based on observed load like CPU or custom metrics — scaling out and in. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts the CPU and memory requests of individual pods — scaling up and down the size of each pod. The Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes whole nodes from the cluster when pods cannot be scheduled or nodes sit idle. KEDA is an event-driven add-on that lets the HPA scale on external signals such as queue depth or Kafka lag rather than CPU, which fits bursty, queue-based workloads that CPU alone reacts to too slowly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's processing floor. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is the policy of opening more identical counters when the queue grows and closing them when it shrinks. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler is the policy of giving each individual clerk a bigger desk and more drawers because the work each one does turned out to need more space than you first allotted. The Cluster Autoscaler is the facilities team that leases another floor of the building when there is no room left for new counters, and gives back a floor when it is empty to save rent. KEDA is the special rule for the back office: instead of watching how hard the clerks are sweating, it watches the physical height of the pile of pending forms and pulls in workers the instant the pile grows, even from zero, which is exactly right for batch paperwork that arrives in bursts.

**One line to remember:** HPA adds more pods, VPA makes each pod bigger, Cluster Autoscaler adds more nodes, and KEDA scales on event signals like queue depth instead of CPU — different layers for different problems.

sections.s2_technical:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler operates on replica count. It watches a metric, classically average CPU utilization but also memory or custom and external metrics, and compares it to a target. If the current value exceeds the target, it computes a higher desired replica count and scales out; if it falls below, it scales in, within configured minimum and maximum bounds. For example, with a CPU target of sixty percent and pods running at ninety percent, the HPA increases replicas until average CPU drops back toward sixty. This is the workhorse for stateless request-serving services, because adding identical replicas both increases capacity and improves availability.

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler operates on pod size, meaning the CPU and memory requests and limits of a single pod. It observes actual resource usage over time and recommends or automatically sets more appropriate requests, so a pod that was under-provisioned gets more and an over-provisioned pod gives some back, which improves bin-packing and prevents both throttling and waste. The important catch is that changing a pod's requests requires recreating the pod, so VPA in auto mode restarts pods to apply new sizes, which is disruptive and is why it suits workloads that are not latency-sensitive to brief restarts, like batch jobs or background services.

The Cluster Autoscaler operates on nodes. It watches for pods that are pending because no node has room to schedule them and adds nodes to the underlying cloud node group, and conversely it removes nodes that have been underutilized for a while, rescheduling their pods elsewhere. It is the layer that makes HPA and VPA actually possible at scale, because adding replicas or growing pods is useless if there is no machine to place them on. For example, when the HPA wants thirty replicas but the current nodes only fit twenty, the Cluster Autoscaler provisions more nodes so the extra ten can schedule.

The crucial interaction question is whether HPA and VPA can be used together. The direct answer is that you must not have both HPA and VPA act on the same resource metric, because they will fight: HPA tries to fix high CPU by adding replicas while VPA tries to fix the same high CPU by enlarging each pod, and the two oscillate. The safe pattern is to let HPA scale on one signal (say CPU or a custom metric) and let VPA manage a different dimension (say memory requests), or to run VPA in recommendation-only mode so a human applies sizes while HPA handles live scaling. On the same metric, pick one, not both.

KEDA, the Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler, addresses workloads where CPU is a poor proxy for how much work is waiting. A consumer draining a Kafka topic or a queue may sit at low CPU while a huge backlog builds, and CPU-based HPA would react slowly or not at all. KEDA scales on the event source directly, for example the number of unprocessed messages or the Kafka consumer-group lag, and uniquely it can scale to zero when there is no work and scale up instantly when messages arrive. Under the hood KEDA drives the standard HPA using these external metrics, so you get event-driven scaling with the familiar HPA machinery. You reach for it for asynchronous, bursty, queue-based processing, while you keep plain CPU or request-rate HPA for synchronous request-serving services. The senior-level framing is that these tools are layered and complementary: HPA and KEDA decide how many pods, VPA decides how big each pod is, and the Cluster Autoscaler decides how many machines exist to hold them.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs two very different workloads: a synchronous transfer API that customers hit directly, and an asynchronous settlement worker that drains a queue of end-of-day settlement messages.

Problem 1 — the transfer API was scaled by CPU, which worked well, but someone also turned on VPA in auto mode on the same CPU metric, and the two autoscalers began fighting, with VPA enlarging pods while HPA added replicas, causing constant restarts and oscillation. This is exactly the HPA-and-VPA-on-the-same-metric trap, and the fix is to let HPA own CPU-based replica scaling and use VPA only for a different dimension or in recommendation mode.

Problem 2 — the settlement worker was also scaled by CPU, but it spent most of its time waiting on input and output, so CPU stayed low even when a huge backlog of settlement messages piled up at market close, and the HPA barely scaled it, so settlements ran dangerously late. This is exactly the case for KEDA: scale on queue depth, not CPU, and allow scaling from zero during quiet hours up to many workers the instant the backlog appears.

Problem 3 — when both workloads scaled out hard at the same time, the existing nodes ran out of room and new pods sat pending. This is exactly the Cluster Autoscaler's job: add nodes so the pending pods can schedule, and remove them later when idle.

The mini-project builds a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` scaling on CPU, a `VerticalPodAutoscaler` recommending pod sizes, a `ClusterAutoscaler` adding nodes for pending pods, and a `KedaScaler` scaling a worker on queue depth including scale-to-zero. The demo scales the transfer API on CPU, shows VPA recommending a size without fighting HPA, scales the settlement worker on queue depth with KEDA, and shows the Cluster Autoscaler adding a node when pods cannot fit.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the autoscaler comparison
java -cp target/classes com.bank.autoscale.AutoscaleDemo

# Apply the real Kubernetes autoscalers
kubectl apply -f k8s/hpa.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/vpa.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/keda-scaledobject.yaml

# Inspect them
kubectl get hpa                         # replica scaling state
kubectl describe vpa transfer-service-vpa   # size recommendations
kubectl get scaledobject                # KEDA event-driven scaling
kubectl get nodes                       # cluster autoscaler adds/removes nodes
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer API whose CPU spikes to ninety percent then cools to thirty, a pod whose observed peak memory is seven hundred mebibytes, a settlement worker whose queue goes from zero to ten thousand messages and back to zero, and a cluster of three nodes holding ten pods each.

Step 1: The HPA reconciles the transfer API at ninety percent CPU against a sixty percent target. Because current CPU is well above target, it computes a higher desired replica count and scales out. When CPU later cools to thirty percent, it scales back in toward the minimum, always staying within its bounds.

Step 2: The VPA observes the pod's peak memory of seven hundred mebibytes and recommends a request of eight hundred ninety-six mebibytes after adding headroom and rounding. Crucially it recommends a memory size and does not touch CPU, so it does not fight the HPA that owns CPU-based replica scaling. In recommendation mode a human applies the size, which requires recreating the pod.

Step 3: The KEDA scaler reconciles the settlement worker at a queue depth of zero. With no work, it scales the worker to zero replicas, saving all resources during quiet hours. This scale-to-zero is something plain CPU-based HPA cannot do.

Step 4: Market close dumps ten thousand settlement messages into the queue. KEDA reconciles against this lag with a threshold of five hundred messages per worker and wakes the worker from zero straight up to twenty replicas, reacting to the backlog instantly rather than waiting for CPU to rise.

Step 5: Once the backlog drains to zero, KEDA scales the worker back to zero. The worker only consumed resources exactly while there was work to do.

Step 6: The Cluster Autoscaler sums all the pods that must run across workloads, finds they exceed the capacity of three nodes at ten pods each, and adds nodes so the pending pods can schedule. When the workloads later shrink and a node sits idle, it removes a node. The summary shows all four autoscalers settled: HPA at its replica count, VPA with a memory recommendation, KEDA back at zero, and the cluster at the node count needed to hold everything.

```

2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    HPA cpu=30% target=60% replicas 5 -> 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are three complementary Kubernetes autoscalers that operate on completely different axes, plus an event-driven add-on. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pod replicas based on a load metric like CPU, so it scales a service out and in. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts the CPU and memory requests of each individual pod, so it scales the size of a pod up and down. The Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes whole nodes when pods cannot be scheduled or nodes sit idle. The simple way I phrase it is: HPA changes how many pods, VPA changes how big each pod is, and the Cluster Autoscaler changes how many machines exist to hold them.

The HPA is the workhorse for stateless request-serving services, because adding identical replicas both increases capacity and improves availability. The VPA is about right-sizing: it watches actual usage and recommends more appropriate requests, which improves bin-packing and prevents both throttling and waste, but the important catch is that changing a pod's requests requires recreating the pod, so VPA in automatic mode restarts pods, which makes it better suited to batch or background workloads than to latency-sensitive request paths. The Cluster Autoscaler is what makes the other two possible at scale, because adding replicas or enlarging pods is useless if there is no node with room, so it provisions nodes when pods are pending and removes underutilized nodes to save cost.

On the key question of whether HPA and VPA can be used together, the honest answer is yes, but only if they do not act on the same resource metric. If both target CPU, they fight: the HPA tries to fix high CPU by adding replicas while the VPA tries to fix the same high CPU by enlarging each pod, and the two oscillate and thrash. The safe pattern is to let the HPA own one signal, typically CPU, and let the VPA manage a different dimension like memory, or run the VPA in recommendation-only mode so a human applies sizes while the HPA handles live scaling. I actually hit this exact trap on a transfer service where both were pointed at CPU and the pods restarted constantly until we separated their metrics.

KEDA is what I reach for when CPU is a poor proxy for how much work is waiting. A consumer draining a Kafka topic can sit at low CPU while a massive backlog builds, and CPU-based HPA barely reacts. KEDA scales directly on the event source, for example Kafka consumer-group lag or queue depth, and uniquely it can scale to zero when there is no work and wake up instantly when messages arrive. Under the hood it drives the standard HPA with these external metrics. On our settlement worker, which was idle most of the day and then flooded at market close, switching from CPU-based scaling to KEDA on queue depth meant it sat at zero cost when quiet and shot up to many workers the instant the backlog appeared, so settlements never ran late again.

The way I summarize it for an interviewer is that these tools are layered and complementary: HPA and KEDA decide how many pods, where HPA fits synchronous CPU or request-driven services and KEDA fits bursty queue-based workloads including scale-to-zero, the VPA decides how big each pod should be, and the Cluster Autoscaler decides how many nodes exist to hold everything. Use them together, just never point HPA and VPA at the same metric.
